rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - one-season (May-Sept 2016) field experiment in Kailu County with TDR soil water measurements in a flood-irrigated and a mulched-drip-irrigated plot, plus Hydrus-2D simulation calibrated on flood-plot data and validated on drip-plot data (Table 4, Fig. 4). Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.4.1/Fig. 5 - simulated bottom-boundary drainage of 20.4 mm under mulched drip vs 55.8 mm under flood; cumulative water fluxes at 1.5-4.0 m depth under flood 1.8-2.7 times those under drip; infiltration depth 325 cm under drip vs 400 cm under flood (Fig. 6); authors conclude mulched drip reduced infiltration depth and groundwater recharge; model output was compared with measured soil water content (NSE 0.35-0.86). Q4: Section 3.1/Fig. 3 measured soil water profiles (lower under drip in main growth stage) and Table 5 simulated water balance showing reduced evaporation (60.2 vs 130.6 mm), lower irrigation input (228 vs 381 mm) and reduced deep fluxes at successive depths (Fig. 5), i.e. the intermediate soil-water pathway to reduced recharge was measured and modelled.
rows.notes: The technology is drip irrigation combined with plastic film mulch compared against flood irrigation, so the recharge difference confounds drip with mulch and with a lower irrigation amount; treated as drip evidence since mulched drip is a drip system. Recharge itself was not measured: it is a model output (drainage at 4 m, free-drainage boundary) from a Hydrus-2D model validated only against soil water content to 150 cm, so no triangulation (Q3). Single site, single crop, single season (Q5 no). Plots were 86 and 71 ha areas but results are point-profile/2D simulations at the plot centre; regional statements are extrapolations (Q6 no). No condition stated as a requirement for the effect (Q7); the note that the simulation ended at harvest and the 400 cm domain cap are not framed as limitations (Q8 no). Only validation errors (MAE, NRMSE, NSE) reported, no dispersion for the recharge result (Q9 no). The text says drip drainage was 'about 2.7 times' flood, but Table 5 shows the reverse (20.4 vs 55.8 mm), apparently a wording error.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - own 2016 field experiment (TDR soil water, two plots, three replications) and Hydrus-2D simulation calibrated/validated against measured soil water content (Table 4, Fig. 4). Q2: Table 5, Figs. 5-6 and Section 4.2/Conclusions - simulated drainage 20.4 mm under mulched drip vs 55.8 mm under flood, smaller cumulative fluxes at 1.5-4.0 m and shallower infiltration depth (325 vs 400 cm) under drip; authors state mulched drip reduced groundwater recharge and that this lowers the water table and threatens the stability of regional groundwater. Q4: Fig. 3 measured soil water content lower under drip in the main growth stage; Table 5 simulated water balance (evaporation 60.2 vs 130.6 mm, irrigation 228 vs 381 mm) and Fig. 5 depth-wise fluxes trace the pathway from reduced input/evaporation to reduced deep drainage.
rows.notes: The 'regional groundwater stability' implication is an inference from a single-site, single-season plot-scale simulation; groundwater levels were not monitored and the recharge value is a model drainage flux validated only through soil water content to 150 cm. Technology is drip plus plastic mulch at lower irrigation amount, so the effect is not attributable to drip alone. No triangulation, no multi-site evaluation, no scale above plot, no stated requirement conditions, no explicit limitations, and no dispersion or uncertainty analysis for the recharge result.

notes: Full text available with figures described by captions. Study is a single-season (2016) comparison of mulched drip vs flood irrigation on maize at one site in the Xiliao River Plain; groundwater recharge differences come from Hydrus-2D simulation (free-drainage boundary at 4 m) whose soil water content output was validated against TDR measurements (NSE 0.35-0.86). Some OCR duplication in the text but no missing sections.
